claim: Obesity and diabetes are established comorbidities for COVID-19.
source: Obesity and diabetes are established comorbidities for COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and is supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adipose tissue demonstrates high expression of ACE2 which SARS-CoV-2 exploits to enter host cells.
source: Adipose tissue demonstrates high expression of ACE2 which SARS- CoV-2 exploits to enter host cells.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the main text (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020; Al-Benna, 2020).

claim: Adipose tissue serves as a reservoir for SARS-CoV-2 viruses, increasing the integral viral load.
source: This makes adipose tissue a reservoir for SARS-CoV-2 viruses and thus increases the integral viral load.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations and in vitro studies mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Acute viral infection results in ACE2 downregulation.
source: Acute viral infection results in ACE2 downregulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and explained mechanistically in the main text through virus-induced endocytosis.

claim: ACE2 deficiency can lead to disturbances in the renin-angiotensin system.
source: This relative deficiency can lead to disturbances in other systems controlled by ACE2, including the renin-angiotensin system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the main text with mechanistic explanations.

claim: Patients with obesity and diabetes have pre-existing compromised functioning of ACE2-controlled systems.
source: This will be further increased in the case of pre-conditions with already compromised functioning of these systems, such as in patients with obesity and diabetes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the main text.

claim: Virally-induced ACE2 deficiency interacts synergistically with obesity and/or diabetes to impair endothelial and gut barrier function.
source: Here, we propose that interactions of virally-induced ACE2 deficiency with obesity and/or diabetes leads to a synergistic further impairment of endothelial and gut barrier function.
evidence: This is explicitly proposed as a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Bacteria and/or their products appear in the lungs of obese and diabetic patients with COVID-19.
source: The appearance of bacteria and/or their products in the lungs of obese and diabetic patients promotes interactions between viral and bacterial pathogens, resulting in a more severe lung injury in COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by post-mortem analysis and clinical studies cited in the main text.

claim: Viral-bacterial interactions result in more severe lung injury in COVID-19.
source: The appearance of bacteria and/or their products in the lungs of obese and diabetic patients promotes interactions between viral and bacterial pathogens, resulting in a more severe lung injury in COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by animal model studies (PRCV model) cited in the main text.

claim: Obesity was one of the most important factors associated with hospitalization and critical illness in COVID-19 patients in a US cohort study of 2741 patients.
source: A prospective cohort study on 2741 patients hospitalized in the US health care system revealed that obesity was one of the most important factors associated with hospitalization and critical illness (Petrilli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with a specific citation to a clinical study.

claim: 41% of 5700 US patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19 had obesity and 33% had T2D.
source: Another US study on 5700 patients hospitalized with severe forms of COVID-19 reported that many of them had either obesity (41%) or T2D (33%) (Richardson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific percentages and citation.

claim: Individuals with obesity in China demonstrate significantly more severe forms of COVID-19 compared to patients with normal weight.
source: According to results obtained in China, individuals with obesity compared to patients with normal weight demonstrate significantly more severe forms of COVID-19 (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation to a Chinese study.

claim: T2D is associated with mortality and severity of COVID-19 with pooled odds ratios of 1.90 and 2.75, respectively.
source: A meta-analysis based on 33 studies revealed that T2D is associated with mortality and severity of COVID-19 with pooled odds ratios of 1.90 and 2.75, respectively (Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific odds ratios and citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: Diabetes is an independent prognostic factor in COVID-19 critical care based on a UK study of 6142 patients.
source: A UK study with 6142 patients indicated that diabetes is an independent prognostic factor in the COVID-19 critical care (Dennis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to a UK study.

claim: Patients with morbid obesity and T2D in Kuwait had odds ratios of 5.18 and 9.38, respectively, for ICU admission.
source: A retrospective study on 1158 patients hospitalized in Kuwait revealed that patients with morbid obesity and T2D were much more likely to be admitted to the intensive care unit, demonstrating odds ratios of 5.18 and 9.38, respectively (Al-Sabah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific odds ratios and citation.

claim: Statistically significant correlations exist between obesity prevalence and COVID-19 deaths across different countries.
source: Statistically significant correlations were found between the officially reported obesity prevalence and the corresponding number of total deaths of patients with COVID-19 in a number of different countries (Ekiz and Pazarlı, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to a cross-country analysis.

claim: A strong negative correlation exists between age and BMI in ICU-admitted COVID-19 patients, suggesting obesity shifts severe COVID-19 to younger ages.
source: A strong negative correlation was found between age and BMI in 265 patients admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU), and it was concluded that obesity can shift severe forms of COVID-19 to a younger age (Kass et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation and includes an interpretation of the correlation.

claim: An increase of visceral fat area by one square decimeter was associated with 22.5-fold increased risk for ICU admission and 16.1-fold increased risk for mechanical ventilation in a German study.
source: A single-center retrospective study from Germany based on computed tomography (CT) measurements of visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue in 30 COVID-19 patients (13 of which had severe forms of disease), revealed that an increase of visceral fat area by one square decimeter was associated with 22.5-fold increased risk to be admitted to ICU and 16.1-fold increased risk for mechanical ventilation (Petersen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific risk ratios and citation to a CT-based study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 clearance is delayed in patients with diabetes.
source: Also relevant to this discussion, SARS-CoV-2 clearance is delayed in patients with diabetes (Chen et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2020b)
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: T2D as a single comorbidity negatively impacts the severity of COVID-19.
source: T2D as a single comorbidity negatively impacts the severity of COVID-19 (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: High fasting blood glucose is an independent predictor for mortality in COVID-19 patients without previous diabetes diagnosis.
source: Additionally, a multi-center retrospective study demonstrated that the high fasting blood glucose is an independent predictor for mortality in patients with COVID-19 without previous diagnosis of diabetes (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to a multi-center study.

claim: Adipose tissue demonstrates higher expression of ACE2 in visceral depots compared to the lungs.
source: In the case of direct interactions with the virus, AT, demonstrating higher expression of ACE2 (especially in visceral depots) compared to the lungs (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020; Al-Benna, 2020), can serve as a big reservoir for viral infections (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: An in vitro study confirms that SARS-CoV-2 virus can infect adipocytes where the virus can persist for extended periods.
source: A recent in vitro study (Institute of Biology, University of Campinas, Brazil) confirms that the SARS-CoV-2 virus can infect adipocytes where the virus can persist for extended periods of time (https://agencia.fapesp.br/adipose-tissue-may-be-a-reservoir-for-sars-cov-2-brazilian-researchers-suggest/33729/).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to a specific in vitro study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can upregulate genes associated with lipid metabolism in lung epithelial cells, including genes involved in regulation of leptin.
source: Additionally, SARS-CoV-2 can upregulate genes associated with lipid metabolism in lung epithelial cells, among others the genes involved in regulation of leptin (Al Heialy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infections modulate lipid metabolism in a similar fashion as observed in the obese or diabetic state.
source: This means that SARS-CoV-2 infections modulate lipid metabolism in a similar fashion as observed in the obese or diabetic state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous observation about gene upregulation.

claim: Adipocytes express ACE2, and this expression increases during adipogenic differentiation.
source: Adipocytes express ACE2, and this expression increases during adipogenic differentiation (Gupte et al., 2008)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: ACE2 expression is further upregulated in the obese state.
source: Adipocytes express ACE2, and this expression increases during adipogenic differentiation (Gupte et al., 2008) and is further upregulated in the obese state (Zhang et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: ACE2 may be shed from adipose tissue into circulation and deposited in the lungs, modifying pulmonary susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: ACE2 may be shed from AT into circulation and can be deposited in the lungs, thereby modifying pulmonary susceptibility to SAR-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on known ACE2 shedding mechanisms.

claim: Plasma levels of angiotensin II are significantly increased in patients with severe COVID-19 and correlate with severity of lung injury.
source: This mechanism could be a compensation for significantly increased plasma levels of angiotensin II (Ang II), which is another RAS member triggering vasoconstrictive responses; such Ang II increases were observed in patients with severe COVID-19 manifestations, in which the measured Ang II levels correlated with the severity of lung injury (Liu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to clinical data.

claim: Dysregulation of RAS was proposed to be the main reason for comorbidity between T2D and severity of COVID-19.
source: Dysregulation of RAS was even proposed to be the main reason for comorbidity between T2D and severity of COVID-19 (Obukhov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal from another group with citation.

claim: Obesity is generally associated with a higher risk of severe viral infections.
source: The main problem is that this phenomenon is not specific for SARS-CoV/CoV2, and obesity was generally associated with a higher risk of severe viral infections (Huttunen and Syrjänen, 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Adiposity was identified as an independent risk factor in H1N1 swine flu, with over 60% of mortality cases in California occurring in obese individuals.
source: Adiposity was also identified as an independent risk factor in H1N1 swine flu: over 60% of all mortality cases caused by this infection in California happened in obese individuals with odds ratios of 2.8 and 4.2 for patients with BMI >40 and 45, respectively (Louie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific percentages, odds ratios, and citation.

claim: Obese individuals with BMI >30 are independently associated with increased risk of respiratory hospitalizations during influenza seasons in Canada.
source: A cohort study performed over 12 influenza seasons in Canada revealed that obese individuals with BMI >30 are independently associated with an increased risk of respiratory hospitalizations (Kwong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to a cohort study.

claim: Mice with high fat diet-induced obesity infected with influenza viruses demonstrated significantly higher mortality and more severe lung pathology than lean counterparts.
source: Similar results were obtained in mice with high fat diet-induced obesity, infected with influenza viruses: these animals demonstrated significantly higher mortality and more severe lung pathology than their lean counterparts (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to an animal study.

claim: Influenza viruses bind viral hemagglutinin to sialylated glycans on the plasma membrane as receptors to infect host cells.
source: Of note, influenza viruses bind viral hemagglutinin to sialylated glycans on the plasma membrane, which they use as receptors to infect the host cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about influenza virus entry mechanism.

claim: Sialic receptors were proposed to be an alternative pathway for coronaviruses to enter host cells.
source: Sialic receptors were incidentally proposed to be an alternative pathway for coronaviruses to enter the host cells (Tortorici et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal with citation.

claim: Increased risk for severe COVID-19 was reported in aged individuals and patients with cardiovascular diseases.
source: Increased risk for severe forms of COVID-19 were also reported in aged individuals and in patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) (Mehra et al., 2020)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: 34% of COVID-19 patients admitted to ICU in the UK were from Black, Asian and minority ethnic groups, despite constituting only 17% of the UK population.
source: For the general UK population, 34% of COVID-19 patients admitted to ICU were in the Black, Asian and minority ethnic groups, although this group constitutes just 17% of the UK population (Barsoum, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific percentages and citation.

claim: The ethnic prevalence in COVID-19 ICU admissions cannot be explained just by cardiometabolic, socio-economic or behavioral factors.
source: Such prevalence cannot be explained just by cardiometabolic, socio-economic or behavioral factors (Raisi-Estabragh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to an analysis.

claim: Patients with obesity and T2D have decreased in-hospital mortality rates connected with multiple pulmonary conditions, demonstrating an 'obesity paradox'.
source: The established comorbidities - obesity and T2D - that are associated with severe outcomes with SARS in COVID-19 appear to contradict the 'obesity paradox', a phenomenon epidemiologically well-established for a number of other diseases. Many studies have determined that patients with obesity and T2D have decreased in-hospital mortality rates connected with multiple pulmonary conditions.
evidence: This is directly stated as an established epidemiological phenomenon.

claim: Survival of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease demonstrated statistically significant negative correlations with BMI values.
source: Survival of patients and the development of severe forms of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, characterized by poor gas exchange and strong inflammation, demonstrated statistically significant negative correlations with their BMI values (Landbo et al., 1999; Chittal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Hospitalized obese patients with pulmonary embolism exhibited lower mortality compared to the reference group with odds ratios between 0.56 and 0.63.
source: Hospitalized obese patients with pulmonary embolism exhibited lower mortality compared to the reference group with odds ratios between 0.56 and 0.63 for different types of obesity (Keller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific odds ratios and citation.

claim: T2D patients develop acute lung injury less frequently than non-diabetic counterparts, with odds ratios ranging from 0.33 to 0.58.
source: T2D patients develop acute lung injury (ALI) a lot less frequently than their non-diabetic counterparts, with odds ratios for diabetes and ALI in various studies ranging from just 0.33 to 0.58 (Honiden and Gong, 2009).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific odds ratios and citation.

claim: Obese individuals with pulmonary arterial hypertension had lower in-hospital mortality than non-obese counterparts with adjusted odds ratio of 0.66.
source: Analysis of records for 18,450 patients with a primary diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension revealed that obese individuals had lower in-hospital mortality than their non-obese counterparts (adjusted odds ratio of 0.66) (Agarwal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific odds ratio and citation.

claim: Application of lipopolysaccharides to non-diabetic mice promoted acute pulmonary inflammation.
source: The application of lipopolysaccharides (LPS), which are the major components of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, to non-diabetic mice promoted acute pulmonary inflammation (Dreymueller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to an animal study.

claim: Diabetic Zucker rats demonstrated reduced lung injury and mortality caused by LPS-induced ALI.
source: In contrast, diabetic Zucker rats demonstrated reduced lung injury and mortality caused by LPS-induced ALI (Wright et al., 1999)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to an animal study.

claim: Diabetic db/db mice developed less severe forms of hyperoxia-induced ALI and exhibited better survival rates.
source: diabetic db/db mice developed less severe forms of hyperoxia-induced ALI and exhibited better survival rates (Bellmeyer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to an animal study.

claim: Mice with high fat diet-induced T2D susceptible to MERS-CoV infection have more severe clinical symptoms and delayed recovery.
source: On the other hand, mice with high fat diet-induced T2D susceptible to MERS-CoV infection have more severe clinical symptoms and a delayed recovery. These symptoms were primarily connected with a more severe lung pathology (Kulcsar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to an animal study.

claim: MERS-CoV shows about 50% genetic identity to SARS-CoV-2 but utilizes dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) instead of ACE2 as its cellular receptor.
source: MERS-CoV shows about 50% genetic identity to SARS-CoV-2 but utilizes dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) instead of ACE2 as its cellular receptor (Muniyappa and Gubbi, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: DPP4 inhibitors are widely used in patients with T2D.
source: Of note, DPP4 inhibitors are widely used in patients with T2D (Drucker, 2020)
evidence: This is stated as established clinical practice with citation.

claim: Initial viral loads in patients with severe forms of COVID-19 are thought to be much higher than in patients with milder forms.
source: The initial viral loads in patients with severe forms of COVID-19 are thought to be much higher than in patients demonstrating milder forms of this disease (Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as a prevailing thought with citation.

claim: Viral loads in upper respiratory samples of COVID-19 patients were found to be equal in asymptomatic and symptomatic cases, but clearance rates differed significantly.
source: On the other hand, viral loads in upper respiratory samples of COVID-19 patients were found to be equal in asymptomatic and symptomatic cases, whereas the clearance rates differed significantly between asymptomatic and symptomatic individuals (Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to clinical data.

claim: Host factors such as age and active comorbidities prompted significantly higher hazard ratios for SARS-CoV infections than viral load alone.
source: Moreover, additional host factors, such as age and active comorbidities prompted significantly higher hazard ratios for SARS-CoV infections than the viral load alone (Chu, 2004).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 binds to ACE2 and induces its endocytosis, leading to internalization of the virus/ACE2 complex and downregulation of cell surface ACE2.
source: SARS-CoV-2 binds to ACE2 and induces its endocytosis, leading to internalization of the virus/ACE2 complex and a downregulation of cell surface ACE2.
evidence: This is stated as an established mechanism.

claim: ACE2 has at least three functions: it negatively regulates RAS, facilitates amino acid transport, and serves as a functional receptor for SARS-CoV/CoV-2.
source: ACE2 has at least three functions: it negatively regulates RAS, facilitates the transport of amino acids through association with amino acid transporters and also serves as a functional receptor for SARS-CoV/CoV-2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ACE2 functions.

claim: ACE2 is widely expressed in different organs and tissues, including lungs and adipose tissue.
source: This enzyme is widely expressed in different organs and tissues, including lungs and AT (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020; Al-Benna, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: ACE2 expression in host cells enables modification of Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which is a vasodilating agent counteracting the vasoconstricting effect of Ang II.
source: Expression of ACE2 in the host cells provides the possibility to modify Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which in turn is a vasodilating agent counteracting the vasoconstricting effect of Ang II through its binding to the Mas receptor.
evidence: This is stated as an established mechanism of ACE2 function.

claim: Reduction of the counter-regulatory axis of RAS promotes the development of fibrosis in different organs and tissues.
source: Of note, the reduction of the counter-regulatory axis of RAS promotes the development of fibrosis in different organs and tissues (McKinney et al., 2014; Cha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: ACE2 expression is upregulated in obesity induced by high fat diet.
source: ACE2 expression is upregulated in obesity, either induced by high fat (Zhang et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2016)
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: ACE2 expression is upregulated by a diet high in sucrose.
source: ACE2 expression is upregulated in obesity, either induced by high fat (Zhang et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2016) or by a diet high in sucrose (Coelho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Enhanced ACE2 expression induced by high fructose feeding may induce adipogenesis.
source: Enhanced ACE2 expression induced by high fructose feeding may even induce adipogenesis (Hernández-Díazcouder et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with citation.

claim: Mice subjected to diet-induced obesity exhibit significantly increased ACE2 gene expression in the lungs.
source: Moreover, mice subjected to diet-induced obesity exhibit significantly increased ACE2 gene expression in the lungs (Al Heialy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: Elevated ACE2 expression is found in the diabetic state.
source: Elevated ACE2 expression is also found in the diabetic state (Rao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: The appearance of T2D is with high probability causally linked to enhanced ACE2 expression based on genome-wide association study analysis.
source: These authors analyzed a large genome-wide association study with almost 900,000 patient records of individuals with T2D and found out that the appearance of T2D is with high probability causally linked to enhanced ACE2 expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a large GWAS analysis with citation.

claim: Reduced ACE2 expression is found in the vasculature of both diabetic animals and humans.
source: On the other hand, reduced ACE2 expression is found in the vasculature of both diabetic animals and humans (Gheblawi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Reduced ACE2 expression can lead to the development of endothelial dysfunction and increased vascular permeability.
source: Such a reduction can lead to the development of endothelial dysfunction and increased vascular permeability.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of reduced ACE2.

claim: Obese patients display vascular endothelial dysfunction resulting from an imbalance in expression of vasodilatory and vasoconstricting agents.
source: Indeed, obese patients display vascular endothelial dysfunction resulting from an imbalance in expression of vasodilatory and vasoconstricting agents (Kwaifa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Viral-induced internalization of ACE2 leads to relative ACE2 deficiency in host cells, which modifies local RAS activity.
source: The viral-induced internalization of ACE2 leads to a relative ACE2 deficiency in the host cells, which modifies the local RAS activity
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism with citation.

claim: Viral-induced ACE2 deficiency is assumed to be especially harmful in patients with a reduction of ACE2 at baseline.
source: The viral-induced internalization of ACE2 leads to a relative ACE2 deficiency in the host cells, which modifies the local RAS activity and is assumed to be especially harmful in patients with a reduction of ACE2 at the baseline (Verdecchia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption with citation.

claim: MMP14 expression levels are strongly increased in the adipose tissue of obese mice.
source: Recently, we have demonstrated that the matrix metalloproteinase MMP14 expression levels are strongly increased in the AT of obese mice (Li and Zhao, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' own work with citation.

claim: Application of LPS substantially reduced the expression level of MMP14 in lungs.
source: Application of LPS substantially reduced the expression level of MMP14 in lungs
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: MMP14-/- mice receiving LPS demonstrated 100% mortality connected with severe lung injury.
source: moreover, MMP14-/- mice receiving LPS demonstrated 100% mortality connected with severe lung injury (Aguirre et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: MMP14 is strongly involved in amelioration of inflammation induced by endotoxins.
source: At the same time, MMP14 is strongly involved in amelioration of inflammation induced by endotoxins (Aguirre et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: ACE2 KO mice exacerbate Ang II-mediated inflammation and myocardial injury via substantial overexpression of MMP2, −9 and −14.
source: Remarkably, ACE2 KO mice exacerbate Ang II-mediated inflammation and myocardial injury via substantial overexpression of MMP2, −9 and −14 (Song et al., 2013)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: MMPs can strongly degrade the extracellular and perivascular matrix.
source: Remarkably, ACE2 KO mice exacerbate Ang II-mediated inflammation and myocardial injury via substantial overexpression of MMP2, −9 and −14 (Song et al., 2013), which can strongly degrade the extracellular and perivascular matrix.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of MMPs.

claim: Double mutant Akita/ACE2 KO mice show loss of ACE2 leading to impaired vascular function and activation of MMP-2, −9, and −14.
source: Experiments with double mutant Akita (murine model for human diabetes)/ACE2 KO mice revealed that the loss of ACE2 leads to impaired vascular function and activation of MMP-2,–9, and −14 (Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: The effect of impaired vascular function and MMP activation was observed only in double mutant Akita/ACE2 KO mice, not in either Akita mice or ACE2 KO mice alone.
source: Importantly, this effect was observed only in double mutant mice, whereby neither Akita mice nor ACE2 KO mice alone demonstrate such changes.
evidence: This is directly stated as an important observation from the cited study.

claim: Non-obese ACE2 KO mice manifest just a mild form of SARS-CoV infection and potently reduced pathological changes in the lungs compared to wild-type counterparts.
source: At the same time, non-obese ACE2 KO mice manifest just a mild form of SARS-CoV infection and potently reduced pathological changes in the lungs compared to their wild-type counterparts (Kuba et al., 2005)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: ACE inhibitors and Ang II receptor blockers, both inducing ACE2 expression, may be beneficial in COVID-19.
source: Different reports state that ACE inhibitors (ACEi) and Ang II receptor blockers (ARBs), both inducing the expression of ACE2, may be beneficial in COVID-19 (Rossi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a claim from other reports with citation.

claim: Application of ACE inhibitors and ARBs can increase the severity of COVID-19 through enhancement of the number of functional receptors for SARS-CoV-2.
source: In contrast, the application of such inhibitors can increase the severity of COVID-19 through enhancement of the number of functional receptors for SARS-CoV-2 on the surface of critical cells.
evidence: This is stated as a contrasting hypothesis.

claim: A cohort of 1200 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found no evidence for increased severity in 399 patients on ACEi/ARBs.
source: A recent report found no evidence for increased severity in a cohort of 1200 hospitalized patients with COVID-19, 399 of which were on ACEi/ARBs (Bean and Kraljevic, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to clinical data.

claim: The odds ratio for severe COVID-19 outcome in patients on ACEi/ARB adjusted for age and sex was 0.70.
source: Moreover, the odds ratio for a severe outcome in patients on ACEi/ARB adjusted for age and sex was 0.70.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the cited study.

claim: Exposure to ACEi's or ARB's induces ACE2 expression but does not influence its shedding from the cell surface.
source: Exposure to ACEi's or ARB's induces ACE2 expression, but does not influence its shedding from the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these drugs.

claim: ACE2 shedding is mainly regulated by ADAM17, which is a tumor necrosis factor-converting enzyme.
source: Such shedding is mainly regulated by Disintegrin and Metalloproteinase Domain 17 (ADAM17), which is a tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-converting enzyme.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: ADAM17 can modulate free ACE2 in circulation.
source: ADAM17 can however also modulate free ACE2 in circulation (Lambert et al., 2005)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: ADAM17 is appreciated as a potential therapeutic target for different inflammatory and vascular conditions.
source: ADAM17 can however also modulate free ACE2 in circulation (Lambert et al., 2005) and is appreciated as a potential therapeutic target for different inflammatory and vascular conditions (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Hyperglycemia induces transcriptional upregulation of ADAM17.
source: Hyperglycemia, typical in T2D, induces a transcriptional upregulation of ADAM17
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Increased ADAM17 protein expression is found in both diabetic patients and diabetic animal models.
source: Hyperglycemia, typical in T2D, induces a transcriptional upregulation of ADAM17, and increased ADAM17 protein expression is indeed found in both diabetic patients and in diabetic animal models (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Hyperglycemic upregulation of Ang II activates ADAM17 through the AT1R receptor, inducing ACE2 shedding.
source: The postulated mechanistic basis may primarily be the hyperglycemic upregulation of Ang II, which subsequently, through the AT1R receptor, activates ADAM17, thereby inducing the shedding of ACE2.
evidence: This is stated as a postulated mechanism.

claim: Ang II levels in circulation of COVID-19 patients were significantly elevated and linearly associated with viral load and lung injury.
source: Ang II levels in circulation of COVID-19 patients were found to be significantly elevated and linearly associated with viral load and lung injury (Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to clinical data.

claim: Dysregulation of RAS associated with ACE2 reduction increases vascular permeability, edema, fibrosis and severity of pulmonary injury through uncontrolled action of Ang II.
source: Dysregulation of RAS associated with the reduction of ACE2 increases vascular permeability, edema, fibrosis and severity of pulmonary injury through uncontrolled action of Ang II (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Overexpression of ACE2 in individuals with obesity and T2D produces a protective effect against Ang II that would otherwise trigger vasoconstriction in the lung.
source: The overexpression of ACE2 as typically found in individuals with obesity and T2D produces a protective effect against Ang II that otherwise would trigger vasoconstriction in the lung.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the known functions of ACE2.

claim: In obese patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus causes a significant increase of Ang II levels that likely cannot be compensated by enhanced ACE2 expression, leading to more severe lung injury.
source: In obese patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus causes a significant increase of Ang II levels in circulation, which very likely cannot be compensated by enhanced ACE2 expression, thereby leading to a more severe lung injury.
evidence: This is stated as a likely mechanism based on inference.

claim: Pulmonary diseases in obesity per se and in obesity combined with viral infections are governed by overexpression of different parts of RAS.
source: In other words, pulmonary diseases in obesity per se and in obesity combined with viral infections, are governed by the overexpression of different parts of RAS.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the evidence.

claim: The differential RAS overexpression is very likely contributing to the 'obesity paradox'.
source: This effect is very likely contributing to the 'obesity paradox'.
evidence: This is stated as a likely explanation.

claim: Suppression of ADAM17 may exert a protective effect on COVID-19.
source: The suppression of ADAM17 may exert a protective effect on COVID-19 (Palau et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with citation.

claim: ADAM17 plays an important role in enabling SARS-CoV/CoV-2 to enter host cells through regulation of fusion of viral particles with cytoplasmic membranes.
source: since ADAM17 plays an important role in enabling SARS-CoV/CoV-2 to enter host cells through the regulation of the fusion of viral particles with cytoplasmic membranes.
evidence: This is stated as an established role with citation.

claim: Application of ADAM17 siRNA reduces SARS-CoV infectivity.
source: Indeed, the application of ADAM17 siRNA reduces SARS-CoV infectivity (Haga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to experimental data.

claim: The number of bacteria that humans carry is estimated to be over 100 trillion, outnumbering the total quantity of human cells.
source: The number of bacteria that humans carry is estimated to be over 100 trillion, which outnumbers by far the total quantity of cells in humans (Velmurugan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an estimate with citation.

claim: Under normal conditions, bacteria have a commensal relationship and can be involved in innate and adaptive immunity.
source: Under normal conditions, these bacteria have a commensal relationship and can even be involved in innate and adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Dysbiosis of gut and lung microbiota is causally involved in the pathogenesis of cardiopulmonary diseases.
source: On the other hand, dysbiosis of gut and lung microbiota is causally involved in the pathogenesis of cardiopulmonary diseases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Modulation of ACE2 can strongly modify the composition of microbiota by influencing amino acid transport and production of antimicrobial peptides.
source: Such dysbiosis is connected to ACE2 expression: modulation of ACE2 can strongly modify the composition of microbiota by influencing the amino acid transport and production of antimicrobial peptides (Cole-Jeffrey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Development of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is directly connected with enhanced presence of Staphylococcus and Streptococcus bacteria in the lung.
source: Moreover, the development of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is directly connected with the enhanced presence of Staphylococcus and Streptococcus bacteria in the lung (Han et al., 2014)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Enteric application of probiotics prevents the development of upper respiratory tract infections.
source: enteric application of probiotics prevents the development of upper respiratory tract infections (Popova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Gut microbiota are recognized as major environmental determinants of obesity and T2D.
source: Gut microbiota are recognized as the major environmental determinants of obesity and T2D
evidence: This is stated as recognized knowledge with citation.

claim: Gut dysbiosis is involved in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance.
source: gut dysbiosis is involved in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance (Kau et al., 2011; Anhê et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Live bacteria and bacterial DNA are long-term constituents in different fat depots in obesity and T2D.
source: A number of recent reports described live bacteria and bacterial DNA as long-term constituents in different fat depots in obesity and T2D (Anhê et al., 2020; Gurung et al., 2020; Massier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations to recent reports.

claim: The presence of bacteria in adipose tissue may be related to decreased barrier function in obese and diabetic individuals.
source: This may be related to the decreased barrier function in these individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: Both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria can be found in human adipose tissues.
source: Whereas the spectrum of bacteria is different in obesity and T2D, both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria can be found in human adipose tissues (Anhê et al., 2020; Massier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Bacteria, bacterial DNA and bacterial products such as LPS are detected in circulation of obese and T2D individuals.
source: Bacteria, bacterial DNA and bacterial products such as LPS are also detected in circulation of obese and T2D individuals (Sato et al., 2014; Velmurugan et al., 2020; Anhê et al., 2020)
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Patients with obesity and T2D suffer from system-wide dissemination of bacteria.
source: which means that patients with these diseases suffer from a system-wide dissemination of bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the detection of bacteria in circulation.

claim: Metabolic endotoxemia (translocation of bacteria-derived LPS into circulation) in obesity and T2D is a matter of intense investigation.
source: The relative physiological importance of metabolic endotoxemia – i.e. the translocation of bacteria-derived LPS into circulation - in obesity and T2D as well as in cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases, is a matter of intense investigation (Cani et al., 2007; Neves et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations indicating ongoing research.

claim: Metabolic endotoxemia was connected to the development of low-grade inflammation through activation of toll-like receptors 4 (TLR4).
source: Metabolic endotoxemia was connected to the development of low-grade inflammation through activation of toll-like receptors 4 (TLR4) (Neves et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Low-grade systemic inflammation (meta-inflammation) was argued to be an obvious reason for high mortality of COVID-19 patients with metabolic diseases.
source: Such low-grade systemic inflammation (meta-inflammation) was argued to be an obvious reason for high mortality of patients with COVID-19 having metabolic diseases (Mauvais-Jarvis, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an argument from another source with citation.

claim: Both viral and bacterial pathogens can activate the TLR4 pathway.
source: Both viral and bacterial pathogens can activate the TLR4 pathway
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Modification of TLR4 signaling is reported to be involved in different viral infections including SARS-CoV.
source: modification of TLR4 signaling is reported to be involved in different viral infections including SARS-CoV (Olejnik et al., 2018)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Modification of TLR4 signaling is involved in LPS-induced acute lung injury.
source: modification of TLR4 signaling is reported to be involved in different viral infections including SARS-CoV (Olejnik et al., 2018) as well as in LPS-induced acute lung injury (Ye and Liu, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: ADAM17 is implicated in shedding of both ACE2 and TLR4.
source: Of note, ADAM17 is implicated in shedding of not only ACE2, but also of TLR4 (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: TLR4 plays important regulatory roles for metabolism under normal metabolic conditions.
source: Even under normal metabolic conditions, we have shown that TLR4 plays important regulatory roles for metabolism (Holland et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2014; Tao et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as findings from the authors' own work with citations.

claim: Several groups drew attention to a possible connection between gut microbiota in healthy individuals and potential severity of COVID-19.
source: It is therefore not surprising that several groups recently drew attention to a possible connection between the gut microbiota in healthy individuals and the potential severity of COVID-19 (Dhar and Mohanty, 2020; Gou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent work.

claim: Some bacteria trigger an intensive response in adipocytes, while others use adipose tissue as a safe haven from the immune system.
source: Some bacteria trigger an intensive response in adipocytes, others seem to use AT as a safe haven, protecting them from the immune system.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental evidence cited below.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters adipocytes and survives inside these cells in a non-replicative state, protected from anti-mycobacterial drugs.
source: Experiments looking into the interaction of Mycobacterium tuberculosis with primary mouse preadipocytes (3T3-L1 cells) and primary human adipocytes in vitro revealed that this pathogen enters adipocytes and survives inside these cells in a non-replicative state, completely protected from anti-mycobacterial drugs (Neyrolles et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to in vitro experiments.

claim: Rickettsia prowazekii can infect and replicate in 3T3-L1 cells, rendering adipose tissue a dormant reservoir for this pathogen.
source: Rickettsia prowazekii (the causative agent of typhus) can infect and replicate in 3T3-L1 cells rendering adipose tissue into a dormant reservoir for this pathogen (Bechah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Coxiella burnetii is found in adipose tissue four months post-infection when no bacteria are detectable in other tissues, making adipose tissue a long-term reservoir.
source: Coxiella burnetii (the agent of query fever) is found in AT even four months post-infection, when no bacteria are detectable in other tissues, thus making AT a safe haven and a long-term reservoir, prevailing even after apparent full clinical recovery (Bechah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Microbiota in adipose tissue likely serve as an additional source for endotoxins.
source: While no direct evidence points to microbiota in AT serving as an additional source for endotoxins, we assume this is very likely.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption by the authors.

claim: Synergistic interactions of diabetes and ACE2 deficiency on endothelial function and MMP overexpression are observed in Akita/ACE2 KO double mutant mice.
source: Similar to the synergistic effects of diabetes and ACE2 deficiency on endothelial function and overexpression of MMPs observed in Akita/ACE2 KO double mutant mice (Patel et al., 2012), synergistic interactions of these two factors are also observed in the modification of gut microbiota and gut barrier function (Duan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Synergistic interactions of diabetes and ACE2 deficiency are observed in modification of gut microbiota and gut barrier function.
source: Similar to the synergistic effects of diabetes and ACE2 deficiency on endothelial function and overexpression of MMPs observed in Akita/ACE2 KO double mutant mice (Patel et al., 2012), synergistic interactions of these two factors are also observed in the modification of gut microbiota and gut barrier function (Duan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Synergism between diabetes and ACE2 deficiency should lead to leakage of pathogens and/or their products from the gut and adipose tissue into circulation.
source: Such synergism should lead to a leakage of pathogens and/or their products from the gut and adipose tissue into circulation.
evidence: This is stated as an expected consequence based on the synergistic effects.

claim: Increase in circulating LPS leads to accumulation of endotoxins in the lung, causing progressive pulmonary inflammation and vascular complications.
source: For example, the increase in circulating LPS will lead to the accumulation of endotoxins in the lung, causing progressive pulmonary inflammation and vascular complications.
evidence: This is stated as an example of the consequence of pathogen leakage.

claim: A large part of LPS in circulation can be neutralized through binding to HDL, resulting in clearance through biliary excretion.
source: Whereas a large part of LPS in circulation can be neutralized through its binding to high density lipoproteins (HDL), resulting in the clearance of LPS through biliary excretion
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: A smaller part of LPS does not associate with HDL and is responsible for activation of macrophages and overproduction of inflammatory mediators.
source: a smaller part of LPS does not associate with HDL and is responsible for the activation of macrophages and the overproduction of potent inflammatory mediators (Vishnyakova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Both HDL and LPS bind to scavenger receptors class B type I (SR-BI).
source: Both HDL and LPS bind to the scavenger receptors class B type I (SR-BI).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: SR-BI receptors belong to a cholesterol delivery system and are present in different cell types, including adipocytes and type two alveolar epithelial cells.
source: These receptors belong to a cholesterol delivery system and are present in different types of cells, including adipocytes and type two alveolar epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to HDL cholesterol.
source: In fact, the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to HDL cholesterol (HDL-C)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: The severity of SARS-CoV-2 infection is inversely associated with plasma levels of HDL-C.
source: the severity of the SARS-CoV-2 infection is inversely associated with plasma levels of HDL-C.
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Antagonists of the HDL receptor SR-BI may inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Surprisingly, antagonists of the HDL receptor SR-BI may inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection (Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a surprising finding with citation.

claim: Patients on statins may be more susceptible to severe forms of COVID-19.
source: Consequently, it may be that patients on statins are more susceptible to severe forms of COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated as a possible consequence.

claim: Multiple studies suggest that individuals on statins may be protected and show reduced rate of mortality in COVID-19.
source: However, multiple studies in the literature have made the case that individuals on statins may in fact be protected and show a reduced rate of mortality (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a contrasting finding from multiple studies with citation.

claim: HDL, non-lipoprotein-bounded LPS and SR-BI are associated with plasma membrane invaginations (caveolae) in different cell types.
source: HDL, non-lipoprotein-bounded LPS and SR-BI were found to be associated with plasma membrane invaginations (caveolae) in different cell types (Vishnyakova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Cholesterol-rich rafts in plasma membrane are substantially involved in penetration of SARS-CoV virus into host cells.
source: This is especially interesting since different authors reported that cholesterol-rich rafts in plasma membrane are substantially involved in penetration of SARS-CoV virus into the host cells (Meher et al., 2019)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Application of methyl-β-cyclodextrin (depleting cholesterol from plasma membranes and destroying caveolae) significantly impairs the efficiency of viral entrance.
source: the application of methyl-β-cyclodextrin (depleting cholesterol from plasma membranes and destroying caveolae) significantly impairs the efficiency of viral entrance (Ren et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to experimental data.

claim: Microbiota can directly or indirectly impact the outcome of different viral infections.
source: It is already established that microbiota can directly or indirectly impact the outcome of different viral infections (Neu and Mainou, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Viruses bind to bacteria through LPS (by Gram-negative bacteria) or peptidoglycan (by Gram-positive bacteria), and this binding can enhance attachment of the virus to its receptor on host cells.
source: Viruses bind to bacteria through LPS (by Gram-negative bacteria) or peptidoglycan (by Gram-positive bacteria), and this binding can provide enhanced attachment of the virus to its receptor on the surface of host cells, thereby enhancing its infectivity (Neu and Mainou, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Virus binding to bacteria can sufficiently increase the integral viral load in the lungs.
source: This effect can sufficiently increase the integral viral load in the lungs.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of virus-bacteria binding.

claim: Respiratory viruses can promote bacterial pneumonia by altering microbiota in the upper respiratory tract and promoting bacterial accumulation in the lower respiratory tract.
source: On the other hand, respiratory viruses can promote bacterial pneumonia, thereby altering the microbiota in the upper respiratory tract and promoting bacterial accumulation in the lower respiratory tract (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Strong synergistic effects of combined coronavirus and bacterial infections on severity of lung injury were demonstrated in the porcine respiratory coronavirus (PRCV) model.
source: Strong synergistic effects of combined coronavirus and bacterial infections on the severity of lung injury was demonstrated in the porcine respiratory coronavirus (PRCV) model (VAN Reeth et al., 2000; Van Gucht et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations to animal studies.

claim: PRCV is common in swine populations and shares several pathogenetic characteristics with SARS-CoV/CoV-2.
source: PRCV is common in swine populations and shares several pathogenetic characteristics with SARS-CoV/CoV-2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Pigs exposed to either PRCV or LPS demonstrated no or only mild symptoms, but combination of PRCV and LPS induced severe SARS in the majority of animals.
source: Combination of PRCV infection with LPS effectively increased severity of SARS: whereas pigs exposed to either PRCV or LPS demonstrated no or only mild symptoms, the combination of PRCV and LPS induced severe SARS in the majority of animals (Van Gucht et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal study.

claim: Synergistic interactions between PRCV and LPS provided hypercytokinemia with about 60 times increase in expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
source: Synergistic interactions between these pathogens provided a hypercytokinemia – a dysproportional (about 60 times) increase in the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid
evidence: This is directly stated with specific fold-change from the cited study.

claim: Hypercytokinemia is typically seen in severe COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission.
source: Synergistic interactions between these pathogens provided a hypercytokinemia – a dysproportional (about 60 times) increase in the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, which is also typically seen in severe COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission (Coperchini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Similar synergistic effects leading to worsening of PRCV infections were observed in combined viral-bacterial infections.
source: Similar synergistic effects leading to considerable worsening of PRCV infections were observed not only for the interactions of viral pathogens with bacterial products, but also in combined viral–bacterial infections (Opriessnig et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Interactions between influenza virus (pH1N1) and LPS in mice resulted in synergistic increase in TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels in lung tissue.
source: Similar results were obtained for the interactions between influenza virus (pH1N1) and LPS in mice: such interactions resulted in a synergistic increase in TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels in lung tissue, promoting a hypercytokinemia and a pulmonary pro-inflammatory immune response (Koch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal study.

claim: LPS induces lung injury through suppression of ACE2 and upregulation of Ang II, ACE, and AT1 receptors, modulating the whole RAS.
source: LPS induces lung injury through the suppression of ACE2 and the upregulation of Ang II, ACE, and AT1 receptors, thus significantly modulating the whole RAS (Ye and Liu, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Factors influencing LPS endotoxicity include enhancers (LPS binding protein and CD14) and suppressors (haptoglobin), all strongly dysregulated in the PRCV model.
source: There are several factors influencing the endotoxicity of LPS, some of them acting as enhancers (LPS binding protein and CD14), others as suppressors (haptoglobin). All these factors are strongly dysregulated in the PRCV model (Van Gucht et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Plasma levels of LPS binding protein are increased in obesity and T2D, demonstrating positive correlation with BMI.
source: On the other hand, plasma levels of LPS binding protein are increased in obesity and T2D, demonstrating a positive correlation with BMI (Sato et al., 2014)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: CD14 expression is enhanced in obese humans.
source: CD14 expression is enhanced in obese humans (Fernández-Real et al., 2011)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Serum levels of haptoglobin are increased both in diabetic rats and in T2D patients.
source: the serum levels of haptoglobin are increased both in diabetic rats (Jelena et al., 2013) and in T2D patients (McMillan, 1989).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Enhanced expression of haptoglobin correlates with serum viscosity and was causally connected with appearance of various microangiopathies in T2D patients.
source: Enhanced expression of haptoglobin correlates with serum viscosity and was causally connected with the appearance of various microangiopathies in T2D patients (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Micro-thrombosis is very common in COVID-19 pneumonia.
source: Importantly, micro-thrombosis is very common in COVID-19 pneumonia (Price et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: ACE2 has a major impact on the composition of gut microbiota.
source: ACE2 has a major impact on the composition of gut microbiota.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: ACE2 modulation by viral infection can significantly influence gut microbiota content and leakage from the gut.
source: ACE2 modulation by viral infection can significantly influence its content and leakage from the gut
evidence: This is stated as an inference from ACE2's role.

claim: Severe forms of COVID-19 were connected with pronounced gastrointestinal symptoms.
source: indeed, severe forms of COVID-19 were connected with pronounced gastrointestinal symptoms (Gou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of twenty COVID-19 patients demonstrated that Enterobacteriaceae spp. were commonly present in lung tissue.
source: Post-mortem analysis of twenty COVID-19 patients demonstrated that Enterobacteriaceae spp., which are abundant in the human gut and can release a large amount of endotoxin, were commonly present in the lung tissue (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to post-mortem data.

claim: A cross-sectional study revealed significantly higher abundance of opportunistic pathogens in gut microbiota of COVID-19 patients compared to influenza A patients and healthy controls.
source: A cross-sectional study of 30 patients with COVID-19, 24 patients with influenza A, and 30 matched healthy controls revealed a significantly higher abundance of opportunistic pathogens in gut microbiota of COVID-19 patients (Gu and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: In a study of 19 patients with severe pulmonary COVID-19, bacterial DNA and toxins were found in blood samples of almost all individuals, with over 40% having high endotoxin levels and over 89% having increased endotoxin levels.
source: In a small prospective study on 19 patients with severe pulmonary forms of COVID-19, bacterial DNA and toxins were found in blood samples of almost all individuals, whereas over 40% of them had high, and over 89% had increased endotoxin levels measured with chemiluminescent-based endotoxin activity assay (Sirivongrangson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with specific percentages and citation.

claim: Bacteria and their by-products in circulation can be translocated to the lungs where they interact with viral infections, worsening the severity of COVID-19.
source: Based on these results, we suppose that bacteria and their by-products in circulation can be translocated to the lungs where they interact with viral infections, producing conditions similar to those observed in the PRCV model and thus worsening the severity of COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated as a supposition by the authors based on the evidence.

claim: Dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity and T2D may be an additional source of bacterial products and likely interacts with viral particles with affinity for ACE2 receptors on adipocytes.
source: Dysfunctional adipose tissue as seen in the context of obesity and T2D may not only be an additional source of these bacterial products, but they are also likely to interact with viral particles with an affinity for the ACE2 receptors on the surface of adipocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a likely mechanism by the authors.

claim: Lung consolidation leading to SARS development is a common complication in COVID-19.
source: Lung consolidation, i.e. regions of lung tissue that are filled with liquid instead of air, leading to the development of SARS, is a common complication in COVID-19
evidence: This is stated as a known complication.

claim: Development of pronounced pulmonary fibrosis is evident in COVID-19 non-survivors.
source: the development of a pronounced pulmonary fibrosis is evident in non-survivors (Zuo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Appearance of pulmonary fibrosis in viral infections is connected with TGF-β overexpression and suppression of ACE2.
source: The appearance of pulmonary fibrosis in viral infections is connected with TGF-β overexpression as well as with the suppression of ACE2 (Zuo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: The authors previously proposed that viral-induced processes can lead to trans-differentiation of pulmonary lipofibroblasts into myofibroblasts, inducing severe pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Recently we have proposed that these processes can lead to trans-differentiation of pulmonary lipofibroblasts into myofibroblasts, thereby inducing severe forms of pulmonary fibrosis and exerting a negative impact on pulmonary gas exchange (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a previous proposal by the authors with citation.

claim: Combined exposure to SARS-CoV-2 and LPS should enhance trans-differentiation of lipofibroblasts into myofibroblasts.
source: If a combination of viral and bacterial infections induces more severe forms of COVID-19, we expect the trans-differentiation of lipofibroblasts into myofibroblasts should also be enhanced under conditions of combined exposure of SARS-CoV-2 with LPS.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation by the authors.

claim: Lipofibroblasts can trans-differentiate into myofibroblasts under different conditions, including hyperoxia and infection.
source: Lipofibroblasts can trans-differentiate into myofibroblasts under different conditions, including hyperoxia and infection (Torday and Rehan, 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Lipofibroblast transformation was connected with deprivation of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) secreted by type two alveolar epithelial cells.
source: This transformation was connected with a deprivation of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), secreted by type two alveolar epithelial cells.
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Application of LPS reduces expression of PTHrP and enhances expression of αSMA, which is the marker of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
source: Application of LPS reduces the expression of PTHrP and enhances the expression of αSMA, which is the marker of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (Torday and Rehan, 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: LPS can lead to trans-differentiation of pericytes into myofibroblasts in renal fibrosis.
source: Similarly, LPS can lead to a trans-differentiation of pericytes into myofibroblasts in renal fibrosis (Castellano et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: LPS-stimulated pericytes secrete LPS binding protein and TGF-β and undergo trans-differentiation even upon TGF-β receptor-blocking, indicating involvement of TLR4 signaling.
source: LPS-stimulated pericytes secrete LPS binding protein and TGF-β and undergo trans-differentiation, even upon TGF-β receptor-blocking. This indicates the involvement of TLR4 signaling (Castellano et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation and interpretation.

claim: Therapeutic application of citrate-based coupled plasma filtration absorption (CPFA) significantly reduced serum levels of TGF-β and LPS binding protein and inhibited trans-differentiation of pericytes.
source: Remarkably, the therapeutic application of citrate-based coupled plasma filtration absorption (CPFA) in this study significantly reduced serum levels of TGF-β and LPS binding protein and inhibited trans-differentiation of pericytes
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to the cited study.

claim: CPFA may be useful in clinical applications to prevent trans-differentiation of lipofibroblasts in COVID-19.
source: which may be also useful in clinical applications to prevent the trans-differentiation of lipofibroblasts over the course of COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated as a possible clinical application.

claim: Intracellular bacteria can induce massive phenotypical changes in host cells.
source: Not only bacterial products, but also the intracellular bacteria themselves can induce massive phenotypical changes in the host cells (Niller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Whether bacterial modifications can cause trans-differentiation of adipocytes and/or lipofibroblasts needs to be investigated in future research.
source: Whether such modifications can cause trans-differentiation of adipocytes and/or lipofibroblasts will need to be investigated in future research.
evidence: This is stated as a question for future research.

claim: The acute inflammatory state in severe COVID-19 is connected to significant hyperglycemia, especially pronounced in patients with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity.
source: The acute inflammatory state in severe COVID-19 is connected to significant hyperglycemia, and this effect is especially pronounced in patients with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity (Gianchandani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Some critically ill COVID-19 patients without diabetes also develop hyperglycemia.
source: Interestingly, some critically ill COVID-19 patients without diabetes also develop hyperglycemia (Gianchandani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation.

claim: Severe hyperglycemia is proposed to be an independent predictor of death and morbidity in various infectious diseases, including COVID-19.
source: Severe hyperglycemia is even proposed to be an independent predictor of death and morbidity in various infectious diseases, including COVID-19 (Apicella et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal with citation.

claim: COVID-19 patients on metformin have better clinical outcomes than patients on insulin.
source: Remarkably, COVID-19 patients on metformin have better clinical outcomes than patients on insulin (Chen et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Insulin administration caused suppression of ACE2 expression in a number of different diabetic mouse models.
source: While insulin administration caused the suppression of ACE2 expression in a number of different diabetic mouse models (Roca-Ho et al., 2017)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: Exposure to pioglitazone significantly upregulates ACE2 expression in different organs and tissues in rats.
source: exposure to pioglitazone significantly upregulates ACE2 expression in different organs and tissues in rats (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: Whether pioglitazone upregulates ACE2 generally remains to be seen, as there is little evidence for this in mice exposed to PPARγ agonists.
source: Whether this is generally true remains to be seen, as we have little evidence for this phenomenon occurring in mice exposed to PPARγ agonists (our unpublished observations).
evidence: This is stated as uncertainty based on the authors' unpublished observations.

claim: PPARγ agonists can modulate endotoxin levels beyond suppression of hyperglycemia and regulation of ACE2 expression.
source: It is very likely that beyond the suppression of hyperglycemia and the possible regulation of ACE2 expression, PPARγ agonists can demonstrate also another effect in COVID-19 patients. These drugs can modulate endotoxin levels.
evidence: This is stated as very likely by the authors.

claim: Use of rosiglitazone in a rat model of bronchopulmonary dysplasia induced by LPS significantly attenuated negative effects of LPS and reduced lung injury.
source: Indeed, the use of rosiglitazone in a rat model of bronchopulmonary dysplasia induced by LPS significantly attenuated the negative effects of LPS and reduced lung injury (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to animal data.

claim: A direct reduction of LPS in circulation was reported in a study of 346 T2D patients treated with different regimens for one year.
source: A direct reduction of LPS in circulation was reported in a study of 346 patients with T2D, which were for one year either diet-controled or treated with metformin, rosiglitazone, a combination of metformin/rosiglitazone or insulin (Al-Attas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to clinical data.

claim: Different PPARγ agonists demonstrated reduction of LPS levels in plasma of treated T2D patients, with most pronounced reductions in the rosiglitazone group and highest LPS values in the insulin group.
source: Whereas different PPARγ agonists demonstrated a reduction of LPS levels in the plasma of treated T2D patients, the most pronounced reductions were observed in the group treated with rosiglitazone, whereas the highest LPS values were found in the group treated with insulin.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited study.

claim: Use of PPARγ agonists (thiazolidinediones) can improve the adipogenic phenotype in lipofibroblasts, reducing their trans-differentiation into myofibroblasts and theoretically preventing pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Additionally, the use of such PPARγ agonists (commonly referred to as thiazolidinediones (TZDs)) can improve the adipogenic phenotype in lipofibroblasts thus reducing the trans-differentiation of these cells into myofibroblasts and theoretically preventing the development of pulmonary fibrosis (Kruglikov and Scherer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical possibility with citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Several pathophysiological mechanisms may be involved in development of severe forms of COVID-19.
source: As we discussed above, several pathophysiological mechanisms may be involved in development of severe forms of COVID-19 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a summary with reference to a table.

claim: Pathophysiological mechanisms can be divided into those connected with ACE2 receptor modulation and those providing viral-bacterial interaction.
source: These mechanisms can be roughly divided in two groups: those connected with modulation of ACE2 receptor (thus directly or indirectly influencing the status of the local or generalized renin-angiotensin system) and those providing an interaction between viral infection and pre-existing bacterial conditions in different tissues as well as in circulation.
evidence: This is stated as a categorization by the authors.

claim: One pathophysiological mechanism should play the predominant role in COVID-19 severity and must be present in all high-risk groups.
source: While all of them can theoretically contribute to the severity of COVID-19, we believe that one of these mechanisms should play the predominant role. Such mechanism must be present not only in obese and diabetic patients, but also in other groups of increased risk in COVID-19, including aged individuals, patients with CVD and some ethnicities.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' belief.

claim: The pathway must be differentially present in males and females and in different ethnic groups to account for gender and ethnicity effects on COVID-19 outcome.
source: Moreover, taking into account multiple reports underlining the influence of gender and ethnicity on the COVID-19 outcome, this pathway must be also differentially present in males and females as well as in different ethnic groups.
